catalog_quote: Words form PHRASES, or stress groups, within utterances. A phrase can be separated from other phrases by pauses and it contains a single stressed word. It is convenient to distinguish two kinds of stress: PHRASE STRESS and WORD STRESS. Phrase stress falls on the stressed word in the phrase (usually the final or penultimate word). Word stress falls on the final syllable of a word. ... This stress …
sweep_summary: Both title-keyword items for Acehnese (Louw & Chateau 2010 'Semantic prosody for the 21st Century'; Louw & Milojkovic 2016 'Corpus Stylistics as Contextual Prosodic Theory and Subtext') are corpus-stylistics works on 'semantic prosody' in English and have nothing to do with Acehnese: Glottolog's own reference pages say the [ace] link is a computerized assignment on the word 'contextual' (the same artefact that attaches five other 'Contextual..' titles to this language). Nothing to acquire from them. The catalog's classification (fixed-dominant, final; deciding source Durie 1984 ANU thesis = Durie 1985 Foris, sec. 2.1 p. 12 and sec. 3.1.2 p. 36, and re-read verbatim) stands. The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Asyik 1987 sec. 1.4.4.2 (held held by the project, re-read): word stress on the last syllable of the stem, never on a suffix/enclitic; phrase stress also right-edge. It confirms and refines (word vs phrase domain) but does not supersede Durie. Two catalog references remain unread and paywalled: Cowan 1981 BSOAS (medium priority; note the DOI recorded in /, 10.1017/S0041977X00144581, is wrong — it resolves to a Klass book review; the correct DOI is 10.1017/s0041977x00144192) and Durie 1995 (chapter DOI 10.1515/9783110884012.1.407, low priority). Crossref, Glottolog, Cambridge Core and archive.org were used instead.

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Acehnese (marked here with (*)) falls on the last syllable of the word but not on the suffix; when a suffix is added to a word, the stress remains where is was, that is, on the syllable before the suffix. bak* 'tree' mate* 'to die' beurangkapat* 'anywhere' meutulak-tulak* 'to push each other'. In a noun phrase or a prepositional phrase, the stress is also on the last syllable (of the last word). ... In a verb phrase the stress is normally on the last syllable too. ... However, when the last constituent is keudeh 'EMP,' a time adverb, or an adverb following a PP, the stress is on the word immediately preceding this constituent.
new_statements.citation: Asyik, Abdul Gani. 1987. A Contextual Grammar of Acehnese Sentences (Complementation). PhD dissertation, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor: UMI; Deep Blue hdl 2027.42/161507). Native-speaker author.
new_statements.locator: Section 1.4.4.2 'Word Stress', printed pp. 27-28 (pp. 49-50; layout the text)
new_statements.reading: Fixed final stress at the word level, with the pronominal 'suffixes' (Durie's enclitics) excluded from the stress domain: stress stays on the last syllable of the stem. Phrase-level prominence is also right-edge (last word of NP/PP/VP), with a few adverbial constituents that push it one word left. This corroborates the catalog's fixed-dominant / final coding and gives the word-vs-phrase separation the catalog's word and phrase together-domain correction was missing: stem-final, not enclitic-final.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations (Durie 1984:12 section 2.1 and 1984:36 section 3.1.2) are verbatim in the held open-access ANU thesis PDF at the stated printed pages (pp. 29 and 53, offset 17 as says). (2) The classification rests on the standard reference grammar of Acehnese (Durie 1984/1985), which is also StressTyp2's own source and the source the Austronesian prosody survey (Himmelmann & Kaufman) cites for Acehnese final/iambic stress; no instrumental or dedicated stress study of Acehnese was found, so nothing better exists. (3) Asyik 1987, the only other substantial modern grammar in Glottolog, was downloaded (open Internet Archive copy) and independently states final word stress, excluding pronominal enclitics, plus phrase-final phrase stress — confirming the classification 'final' (final stress). (4) Status well-sourced. Suggested action: the record's evidence-grade field is blank

sources.quote: "In Acehnese word stress is upon the final syllable. The phonological form of final syllables is invariant: no morphophonemic rules affect final syllables." (Durie 1984:12, section 2.1); "Word stress falls on the final syllable of a word. Thus /ia'/ 'water', /pa#de'/ 'rice', /mw#na#Sah'/ 'meeting house'. This stress is realised when a word is pronounced in its citation form, or when it is the stressed word in a phrase." (Durie 1984:36, section 3.1.2)
